Week 4 rhetorical situation 5.2
A team of people from DisplayWorks have prepared to answer questions on a 15 minute phone conference with Doreen, a potential client at Canadian Radiant Heat Specialist in regard to their Request for Proposals. The RPF from Canadian Radiant Heat Specialists states the need for a sales display unit providing an overview of their products, but concentrated on their newest product, a radiant floor heating system. This sales display would be for the North American construction trade show event held in the March in Las Vegas.
With 6 members on the team, each possesing different roles and specialties they are tasked to organize and manage the top concerns/priorities of the clients needs. While brainstorming ideas the group begins to bicker thus pulling their focus away from the assignment. In my opinion the beginning of the discussion lacked structure and leadership until Bob took it upon himself to do so, and each team member is too busy drawing attention toward their own questions regarding their expertise for the display that they loose sight of the bigger picture. Instead of attempting to reach a resolution the team members wasted what little time they had disagreeing and making unnecessary remarks toward one another. It wasn't until Bob stepped into the spotlight as the leadership role that each person started to reflect, observe, communicate, and prepare for the upcoming teleconference.

For the next rhetorical situation, we are supposed to analyze the group dynamics and describe what is happening within the group.
The team at DisplayWorks is attempting to prepare for a quick meeting with Doreen, a potential client, to look over her request for proposal. The goal of this meeting is to clarify the proposal so that when the group disperses, everyone has a clear path to success on project. What is happening here is there is not a clear process or agenda to keep the group on topic. Additionally, not everyone came to the meeting prepared with their questions, and now the group is scrambling to make sure this short 15 minute phone call covers every important aspect of the project.
There was not an agreeable solution until Bob noticed that tensions started to rise and people started to butt heads. He jumped into action by delegating: asking Amita to bump the meeting to a later time, asking Brianne to go over her vision of the display to gather more follow up questions, asking Luanne to organize and rank everyone's top three questions, and then assigning everyone time to speak at the meeting. These were all helpful things to do, however, next time it would be helpful if Bob (or whoever has the authority) creates a meeting agenda & assignments and sends it to the group ahead of time with instruction on what to prepare for. If Bob does this ahead of meetings from now on, it will help mitigate the panic and frustration they felt in this situation. It is usually a good idea to have a clear plan for meetings with this many people.
In our discussion I believe we need to make suggestions on what all could have been handled better/more effectively.

In this scenario Sunita is a new employee at XXL Advertising sales. She is very frustrated and upset because while using her personal electronics such as her phone and computer XXL required to have passwords to get access to her work email. Damien is able to fix the problem however, in order to resolve the issue, he has to access the security requirements which Sunita feels is not fair since it's her personal devices.
From the company's point of view, they believe the security measures are necessary. Advertising companies are known to handle their client's sensitive information, and unsecured devices could cause serious legal trouble leading to the possible damaging of the company's reputation. Damien takes the necessary steps in trying to resolve the issue by letting Sunita communicate her concerns to management.
In this scenario I believe the best way to handle the situation is by giving the employee the option to either use their own devices or being issued a company device. Personally, I would most likely choose having a company device instead of using my own. One other way this situation could be resolved is if management possibly implements another security device such as biometric authentication. In conclusion the security measurements may seem unnecessary and inconvenient, however it is justified because the company has a responsibility to protect sensitive information.

This scenario involves Sunita Mensah, a new employee at XXL Advertising Sales, and Damian Tucker, another employee. Sunita is having trouble getting her laptop and smartphone to connect to her work email and she asks Damian for his assistance. Damian’s suggestions all involved securing the devices so that in the event that Sunita lost her device, the company and client’s information would be protected. Sunita felt that this was overkill and a hindrance to her using her devices outside of work. Damian told Sunita that he would email the manager of information technology in order to work things out for her.
Damian and Sunita need to be able to respectfully communicate their concerns without trying to put Sunita and her desires above other employees of the company. There are two ways that I see this problem being solved; First, the company could give employees the option of using their own devices or using company provided devices. Depending on the employee, there could be a draw to either choice. As mentioned, most people are more comfortable with their own devices, but with the option to use a company device, it is easier to separate work and personal time. Second, the company could tell Sunita that this is what is expected of their employees and if she wants to work for XXL Advertising Sales she must keep her devices secured.
Damian should write an email explaining Sunita’s concerns. If I were Damian, I would make sure that the tone of my email is respectful and I would not want it to seem like Sunita is above all of the other employees who have made this situation work.

In my time working for a company that acts as a vendor to advertising agencies, I have learned firsthand that advertising companies are extremely cautious when handling not only their own data, but more importantly the data of their clients.
An advertising agency is tasked with both the creation and delivery of an advertising campaign. The delivery requires total secrecy and coordination involving non disclosure agreements, media embargo and, most relevant to Sunita Mensah and Damian Tucker, demanding data encryption standards. Simply put: if information on a client's advertising campaign leaks, the advertising agency is liable for damages, legal remedies could be pursued, and prospects will be more cautious about working with them in the future.
With significant amounts of intellectual property at stake, it would not be rational to allow an employee (much less an inexperienced employee) to access company email on a device that anyone can easily gain access to. If Sunita is to use her own device, she needs to comply with necessary security standards.
If Damian is to write an email in order to challenge this corporate standard, he and Sunita must be willing to compromise in order to ensure the security of company and client data. For instance, facial recognition or fingerprint keys may be viable alternatives. Most of all, both parties need to acknowledge the importance of securing intellectual property and protecting the company; failure to do so would certainly result in a negative outcome.

Hi everyone!
I will make an attempt at mapping out what we need to address to reach our solution:
Damian is going to reach out to the Information Technology manager at XXL Advertising Sales on behalf of Sunita.
I think the first step is to think about what the goal/purpose of the message is. Are we informing or persuading? Is the goal that XXL should make an exception and provide Sunita with the technology she needs to do her job? Is the goal to simply be kind and pass along her frustrations? Or is the goal to start a higher-level conversation about the "bring your device to work" practice within the organization? Is it something else entirely? Figuring out the goal will help us know if we need the Information Technology manager and/or Sunita to take action.
Once we settle on our goal, there are other aspects we need to consider. We do not know what position Damian holds but I will make the assumption he is not in management since it is not stated. Since he is planning to contact a manager about an issue, we should consider their level of authority when we communicate with them. We should also consider obstacles or objections the IT manager could pose, and how their responsibilities, attitudes, and experiences may affect their response. For example, is there a financial aspect Damian doesn't know about that requires employees to use their own devices regardless of circumstance?

This writing scenario is focused on workplace communication issues with bring your own device environments. Sunita Mensah is a new employee in XXL Advertising Sales and is experiencing issues connecting her personal laptop and smartphone with the company's email system. Technical Support works to resolve the issue, however, concerns are rising with security, privacy, and encryption with devices.
The main members in this situation would be Damian and Sunita. Sunita, a new graduate, has less than 6 months at this new company. Which means, she has limited power and learning the workplace systems. The main stake she has is obviously this new job, as well as, the control over her personal devices. Damian is a tech support employee and although he does not carry management pressure he is expected to keep things in line and keep policy requirements in check. The company could also be held responsible for any issues that pop up from this given it's their job to keep their employees safe from any dangerous issues that could come up in the tech department.
The power dynamic of this situation plays a strong role. Sunita owns the devices but being a new employee she would feel pressured and more vulnerable to how the company handles technological security.
Each person has their own interests, Sunita is more likely to value convenience and efficiency, while Damian and the company are prioritizing data security and reducing risk. Understanding each one of these roles is important to effective communication in the given situation.

This situation really highlights the challenges of BYOD in the workplace. Sunita’s lack of power as a new employee puts her in a vulnerable position, especially when her personal devices are involved. It makes sense that she would value convenience and efficiency, while Damian and the company focus more on security and risk prevention. The power dynamic definitely affects how comfortable Sunita feels speaking up. Overall, understanding each person’s role and priorities is key to maintaining effective and fair communication in this situation.

One option to expound on this reaction is to inquire how Sunita's tendency to push back or ask questions is impacted by the power imbalance. It effectively highlights the important figures and power dynamics. If Damian's job should have more power or flexibility when dealing with new recruits who feel overworked, that is another worthwhile topic for debate. The committee may also examine the relationship between personal device ownership and business accountability, particularly in cases where privacy or legal concerns emerge. A fourth suggestion is to take into account how the empathy and communication style of IT personnel may affect new hires' perceptions of intrusive security measures.

Hello everyone,
From my perspective of being the solution designer, I think the core problem in the scenario is the tension between convenience for employees and security requirements for the organization. While bringing your own device into work can save costs from the company not needing to buy private devices, they can also create a serious risk relating to data security, privacy, and control of company information.
I think the company should respond by creating a more clear and practical policy. First, XXL Advertising Sales should use tools that separate personal and work data on devices. This would allow the company to protect their information without interfering with their employees' personal information. Second, the organization should provide better explanations and trainings during the employee onboarding process so the employees can understand why security measures like encryption and strong passwords are necessary. If the employees understand the purpose, they are less likely to feel mad or frustrated.
We also need to address the root problem in this situation, which is the gap between what employees expect and what the organization requires for security. The solution should not only fix Sunita's immediate issue but also prevent similar problems in the future. By combining clear policies, technical solutions, and better communication, the company can protect its data while still supporting employee productivity and comfort.
Let me know what you think or if you guys have any questions!!

I 100% agree that the root problem is the gap between what employees expect and what the organization requires for security. That's why I believe the tone of the message should be more empathetic but also team oriented. You made a good point when you said the organization should provide better explanations and trainings during the employee onboarding process so the employees can understand why security measures like encryption and strong passwords are necessary. But also explain their understanding on why the employees may feel the way do they when using their own device.

Examining how XXL may strike a balance between security and employee workload, such as modifying password timeouts or providing biometric choices if possible, is one method to further this concept. Another helpful perspective is if the business should provide employees who would rather have fewer constraints the option to choose between using their own devices and utilizing a company-issued device. Talking about accountability—who is in charge if a gadget is misplaced or hacked, and how clearly that obligation is conveyed—may also be beneficial. Examining if regular training or brief refresher courses would be more beneficial than one-time onboarding explanations is a fourth possibility. Lastly, in order to ensure that rules change in tandem with actual experience, the committee should think about how employee input, such as Sunita's concerns, should be explicitly integrated into IT policy reviews.

"Rhetorical Situation 5.2: Understanding Group Dynamics: DisplayWorks Prepares for a Client Conference Call Bob looks around the conference table and decides to get started. Doreen over at Canadian Radiant Heat Specialists, their potential client, has agreed to a 15-minute call to answer questions about their Request for Proposals (RFP). They have to make the most of this opportunity. Canadian Radiant Heat Specialists needs a sales display unit for the main North American construction trade show held in Las Vegas in March. The RFP notes that they want the display to provide an overview of their products, but also to focus mainly on their newest product, a radiant floor heating system that uses “hot water conveyed through flexible piping in the floors to heat the structure.” DisplayWorks manufactures custom trade-show display units consisting of collapsible lightweight matrix-like structures with magnetic plastic panels that adhere to the structure. The plastic panels are often graphically rich. Some of the panels are fabric, so brochure holders as well as laminated changeable content can be attached to them with Velcro. The client usually has up to six sales representatives at the trade show, circulating around the booth and interacting with clients, distributing product information, and giving out branded swag and other types of promotional items. These trade-show display units can cost between $25,000 and $50,000, and they are usually about eight meters long and two meters high. They can be disassembled fairly quickly and transported from one show to the next in lightweight plastic cases. DisplayWorks has created display units for a variety of different companies across North America. Everyone around the conference table looks at the RFP, focusing on the part of the description that most closely matches their own expertise. There are six participants: Brianna, the graphic artist in charge of the unit’s design; Bram, the structural engineer in charge of its materials and construction; Amita, Bob’s administrative assistant, who will manage the conference call; Luanne, the chief writer, who will draft the proposal; Victor, the programmer and technical support wizard who will coordinate the electronic display; and, of course, Bob, the salesman at DisplayWorks, who has brought this team together to help prepare the proposal. Victor speaks first, noting that the client wants a computer-controlled flat-panel display and slideshow to present their product details and description, so he needs to know who is going to be running this booth. How technically savvy are they? Does he need to set up this show as an endless loop or should it be indexed so that employees can locate a specific section to show a customer? Brianna agrees and says that presumably DisplayWorks will be producing the presentation for the flat screen. She wonders aloud about the kind of access to Radiant Heat’s manufacturing process that she and her group will have to create the video. Bob replies that he is not sure whether Brianna’s group is creating the video. The RFP isn’t clear on that point. They both agree that this issue is something that needs to be cleared up at the start of the conversation, because production of the video will be time-consuming and potentially costly. Brianna nods and asks whether anyone knows the company colors. Amita said she visited Canadian Radiant Heat Specialists’ website and made copies of their logo and homepage. They use a kind of pumpkin and hunter green in their logo. “Oh,” interjects Brianna, raising an eyebrow. “That doesn’t give us the best palette of colors to work with, but if we use variations of....” Her voice trails off as she begins jotting down notes in the margins around the company logo. Everyone watches her for a few seconds, waiting for her to finish her sentence, but she keeps writing and then turns the paper over and begins drawing on the back. Bob shrugs and looks at the other members of the team. “Any more questions? What about you, Bram? You haven’t said anything. Is the RFP that clear on their structural requirements?” Bram acknowledges that he could use a little more clarity about the size and nature of the content they want to display. He points to the RFP and notes that in the second paragraph, it sounds as if they want posters and digital photos of their products, but on page two, they are also talking about having a selection of actual products on site to handle. He has questions about where they want to display and store those products—on site or in a secure location off site. Also, he needs to know if they want to display some of the products on the unit itself, which will affect the unit construction. The more weight placed on the unit, the better designed and braced it needs to be so it won’t tip over. The conversation continues for several minutes, with Bram explaining the technical aspects of unit construction and the others asking questions and making suggestions. Luanne takes notes of the conversation. Amita asks Bram, Brianna, and everyone else to write down the actual questions that they want to ask because 15 minutes isn’t very long. They need to ensure that they cover the most important questions first, and then if there’s time left over, the ones of lesser importance. She asks them to rank-order their questions and be as concise and clear as they can. Bob decides that the group hasn’t gotten very far in this discussion. He suggests that they try individually brainstorming a list of issues or problems that each person sees with this proposal from the perspective of the area that they will be responsible for in this project. A groan comes from Bob’s right. “Why can’t we brainstorm as a group?” suggests Victor. “That way I don’t have to write everything down twice.” “I already did that,” laughs Bram, a bit smugly. “It was part of my preparation for this meeting to write down the questions that I have about this RFP. I would have thought the rest of you would have gotten prepared before coming too.” “Well, not all of us are single and can devote every waking moment to our job,” retorts Brianna, glaring at Bram. “I did prepare, by the way. I just didn’t write everything down because I can’t drive and write at the same time.” “What about red lights?” jokes Luanne. “My boss at Jazco answered letters by scribbling in the margins while she waited at red lights.” Bob sees the discussion going off track, so he intervenes by pointing out that they are supposed to place the call to Doreen in less than 10 minutes and they aren’t organized yet. Victor suggests rescheduling the conference call, and after some discussion, Bob asks Amita to try to reschedule the meeting for 11:30, giving the group an extra half-hour to organize themselves fully. Bob then suggests that Bram check out the sketch that Brianna has just finished to see if he can foresee any possible structural problems with the design. Then he directs the rest of the group to brainstorm at least three questions that they have about the RFP. After a few minutes, he gestures for the writers to pass their questions forward to him, and then asks Brianna to present her ideas for the display unit. In 15 minutes, Brianna’s initial idea is quickly modified with input from Bram and Victor into a workable model over which the team expresses general satisfaction. During this time, Amita returns, announcing that the meeting has been successfully rescheduled for 11:45 a.m. While she was gone, Bob passed the group’s questions over to Luanne, who reviewed them, rewrote two or three to make them clearer and more pointed, and then rank-ordered them according to complexity and importance. She now reads the questions aloud, noting who she has assigned to read them during the conference call. Victor and Brianna each add follow-up questions to the ones they were assigned. Luanne drafts a schedule on the whiteboard of the order in which each person will speak, how much time they can allot to each question, and what else they should ask if they finish up a bit early. “Terrific work, everyone,” announces Bob with satisfaction. They have a workable plan and a few minutes to practice their execution before placing the call."

For this week's prompt, we have to plan to make the most out of this meeting while also address the long-term organizational problem here.
It sounds like we believe that the team was generally ill equipped with how exactly to move forward with this meeting. Perhaps a leader should have stepped in and briefly discussed it as it sounds like the team feels inexperienced and not very confident regarding this meeting. Despite not being overly prepared, it seems that the teams main issue is lack of organization to discuss questions and thoughts regarding this meeting and generally lacked cohesion.
We know that an outline for this meeting has been developed after pushing the meeting back and people have been delegated certain meeting roles. This helps to control the flow and organization of questions and ideas in the meeting. It sounds like we all strongly believe that 2 major things should have been done here:
A team leader (most likely Bob) should have been identified to make sure everyone was prepared with comments or concerns before the meeting and even possibly given more information as well or at least dedicate time for each of the team members to discuss the meetings together and go over any questions they had.

Week 4 threw a long one at us, so let's begin.
First, the things that we will need to discuss. I see two of you have posted already—thanks! I will read your replies and respond.
Your summary of the events in this weeks prompt should include concepts discussed in chapter 5. Things such as methods of collaboration, group behaviors that lead the team for success and failure, conflict resolution, etc. with evidence to support it. Then interpret what happened (give your input) and discuss why it might have happened. You'll want to identify aspects that worked well and others that did not. The last line in the prompt directions says to suggest ways that the meeting may have been handled better.
The goal is to make the most out of the 15-minute time window Bob and Co. have with Doreen, as the objective is to secure a client for which they can provide a sales display for a trades show.
At first glance, the team seems to work well together. They ask questions to clarify any unknown information. While some of the questions make sense to start, the questions eventually taper off into topics that will not be beneficial for this call, such as the company colors. At this point, the purpose of the meeting is to talk about the RFP and come up with questions and topics that need to be explored with Doreen. Brianna then goes off and does her own thing, something that costs the group time, something they have very little of. Even though this was her assigned role, I believe doing something on her own without the input of the group (until later on, that is) cost the group too much time and caused everyone to begin losing sight of the purpose of the meeting, thus actively listening to everything going on and not isolating oneself at an important time would have been more beneficial.
I found it interesting that it was said that Amita was going to lead the call, but Bob took charge. As the leader, Bob should have specified what was needed of the group and made a timeline or list of achievable goals for the meeting.
At one point, Brianna takes a personal jab at Bob for suggesting the team members did not prepare; this is always a bad idea when collaborating as a team towards a shared goal. When attacking someone personally, it always leads to defensiveness, which is both not the point of the meeting and creates more issues down the line within the group. Luanne cracked a joke at one point, attempting to relieve tension and put everyone in a relaxed state.
The issues the group had happened for more than one reason. The biggest reason, at least to me, was the lack of direction and defined outcome. If the group had some sort of clearly-defined end goal for the meeting going in, they would have been focused and would have been able to work together better. In addition, devising an approach to prepare beforehand would have solved some of the bickering that happened between the group members.
At the end of the day, a shared vision as to what needed to happen was mandatory and because it was neglected, the meeting began rough and took an unproductive turning point before it reached its end goal.

Week 4 Prompt:
When I read the prompt and tried to analyze this situation, I saw team that didn’t have a unified plan from the start. I think that could mean that whoever assembled or managed the group sent them in without clear objectives, training/guidance, or a shared understanding of how to achieve their objective (rfp). Though, I think it could also be that the team was made up of strong individual minds who were used to working and succeeding independently and so they assumed their own strategies would also work in a team setting. Regardless of what the true catalyst for their issues was, the facts show a lack of cohesion. For example, everyone immediately focused on their own section of the RFP, or provided ideas that seemed to fit their own desirable outcomes.
Brianna checked out by sketching while the group waited. Bram brazenly became critical of others for not preparing. Not only was the team ill prepared, but the moments like those show how their team lacked comradery  and wasn’t aligned to begin the process. Without respect for the process and for each other, a collective goal was always at risk of being lost.
I think the facts also show that roles were not designated beforehand. In team communication theory, role clarity is heavily encouraged, if not entirely necessary. Pre-defined roles can be rehearsed and issues can be confronted before true application. They help to prevent overlap, confusion, and competition. In this story, no one knew who was responsible for what. In any team, it's crucial to understand what your roles are as an individual as well as member of a collective whole. I believe this is why Victor questioned who would run the booth, Brianna questioned who would produce the video, and Bram questioned the structural requirements. One question is troublesome, but multiple questions involving numerous members means their is clear confusion and lack of coordination. If roles and objectives had been assigned beforehand, then the group as a whole would have benefited in many ways. Teams don’t often ask that every single member is doing the exact same thing. They also need to all be working toward the same outcome.
In all, my interpretation is that there was very little experience within the team when it came to handling RFPs and trade‑show logistics. I also believe that whoever was responsible for preparing the team did not supply the support and resources needed to have them suited for their tasks. They had to adjust on the fly once conflict and confusion became apparent. They simply weren’t prepared, roles were unassigned, and there was a clear lack of firsthand experience and application of what training they had received. To put it bluntly, they weren't ready to do their jobs. The fact that Bob had to step in, reschedule the call, and direct everyone to write and rank their questions shows that the team couldn't handle finding a solution on their own in a timely manner.

The goal of this discussion is to summarize the way in which we would write an email to the the IT manager conveying the concerns that Sunita has. Conveniently, I am currently employed in and studying IT; I can provide a real-world perspective and application to this topic.
Sunita dislikes the idea of having to have type passwords into her personal devices once they are have been encrypted. This is a very common practice in IT that is one of the many layers in the multi-faceted approach that safeguards networks and data. Realistically, in BYOD policies, devices are enrolled into mobile device managers (MDM) that allow IT departments to monitor location, logins, and many other things. Additionally, the device will be partitioned into two parts: the personal part and the work part. The personal part will host all the data that is yours. The work part will have all the sensitive information on it (think client information, student information, PII, etc.). This section of the laptop will be encrypted and monitored. In the event the device is lost or stolen, using the MDM, the work portion of the device will be remotely wiped; that is, the data will be erased to ensure no one will have access to it. Depending on the policy, companies will modify their approach, but this is industry standard for BYOD.
What we're looking for is a way to approach the IT manager and present Sunita's concern in a way that will not immediately be thrown away. Generally in IT, if you simply ask to bypass a policy you will be denied and any further attempts will not be heard. As such, we'll want to frame Sunita's concern in a way that will give her the opportunity to be heard. For example, I like it when my end users tell me what could be done alternatively to what they do not want. That is, we can ask the IT manager for an alternative solution. For example, asking to provide the devices Sunita will need instead of forcing her to use her own device. This is something mentioned in the prompt, so it's something worth discussing.
